items.title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.original_title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.summary: Carriers Have Returned to Suez, and the Data Confirms It Maritime media sources state that container shipping is moving from a capacity shortage to a surplus as carriers return to Suez and shorter voyages free up ships. Suez containership transits rose 59% from March to September, from 139 to 221. The growth came from large ships, 300m and above, up to 24,000 TEU, the post-Panamax to ultra-large vessels used on main Asia-Europe services, which rose from 22 to 127 transits a month. Around 100 more large containerships now transit the Suez Canal instead of around Africa, compared to March, cutting one to two weeks off each round trip. Suez routing for Asia-Europe services has recovered to only about a quarter of pre-crisis levels, per Sea-Intelligence. Even a partial return matters, because carriers expanded Asia-Europe capacity by approximately 41% between May 2023 and May 2025 to cover the longer route around Africa, according to Alphaliner, meaning that every service that switches back to Suez frees ships the route no longer needs. Shorter voyages mean each liner service needs fewer ships to keep its schedule, freeing capacity just as Europe-bound demand softens after the summer and ahead of China’s Golden Week holiday (1-7 Oct), when factory closures halt much of China’s export production.

items.title: Tankers enter the death zone
items.original_title: Tankers enter the death zone
items.summary: Like climbers entering the death zone above 8,000 metres en route to the summit of Everest, VLCCs have entered their own peak: the moment where prices for secondhand tonnage surpass newbuild prices, and sell signs flash hard. These moments tend to be fleeting and have historically been associated with the hottest stages of shipping cycles. The question is how often the market has reached this altitude before, and how long it can survive there. The previous maximum premium for a five-year-old VLCC over a newbuild was 21% in December 2007. Veson data shows a 15-year-old VLCC overtook the newbuild value for the first time on September 27. Danish Ship Finance takes a broader approach, using a monthly secondhand-to-newbuilding price ratio for tankers stretching back to January 2000. Its series identifies 11 distinct episodes, including the current one. “To stay with your analogy: the death zone usually punishes those who linger — but in 2003–08, the market camped up there for nearly six years,” Danish Ship Finance told Splash. The completed episodes have averaged around 12 months, although that number is heavily distorted by the extraordinary 2003-08 supercycle, which accounts for more than half of all the months its tanker index has spent above parity.

Another 12 orders were for ethanol-fuelled bulk carriers, while nine LPG-fuelled vessels were ordered during the month. DNV warned in its latest Maritime Forecast to 2050 that regulatory outcomes could significantly change the economics of alternative fuels over the operating lives of vessels ordered today. China Daily via REUTERS Ships are being forced to wait significantly longer to refuel at China’s top bunkering hub of Zhoushan, where the fallout from the US-Iran war has tightened supplies and pushed up prices. Some vessels seeking to refuel at the port south of Shanghai are facing wait times of around one to two weeks, according to people familiar with the matter. Spot prices for very low-sulfur bunker fuel sold at Zhoushan on Tuesday were near their highest level since March, in the early days of the Iran war, according to bunker data provider ClearLynx LLC. China’s state-owned refiners produced 1.12 million tons of low-sulfur fuel oil in August, a 13% decline from July, according to data from energy information provider JLC. Beijing has long sought to build Zhoushan into a regional bunkering hub to rival Singapore, though the city-state still remains the clear leader for ship refueling. items.title: Supreme court clears way for Świnoujście deepwater container terminal
items.original_title: Supreme court clears way for Świnoujście deepwater container terminal
items.summary:
Poland's Supreme Administrative Court in Warsaw has dismissed a cassation appeal brought by the German environmental association Lebensraum Vorpommern against the planned deepwater container terminal in Świnoujście, the Szczecin and Świnoujście Seaports Authority announced. The appeal had challenged the project's environmental approvals through the Polish administrative courts, and its dismissal ends that line of litigation, removing one of the main legal obstacles to construction.

The terminal, now branded Cape Pomerania (Przylądek Pomorski), is designed to let the port handle the largest ocean-going container vessels and lift Poland's container capacity on the western coast. The court decision completes the environmental and administrative review process in the Polish judiciary. The announcement did not add new details on specifications, timetable or investment value beyond what the port authority has published before.
items.why: Removes a legal risk to the largest investment in the Szczecin–Świnoujście complex; expect the construction timetable, hinterland traffic and competitive landscape around Świnoujście to firm up.

items.title: EU proposes overhaul of maritime ETS, MRV and FuelEU, extending carbon costs to smaller cargo ships
items.original_title: EU proposes overhaul of maritime ETS, MRV and FuelEU, extending carbon costs to smaller cargo ships
items.summary:
The European Commission's July 2026 proposals would reshape the rules for maritime emissions, targeting a 90% cut in shipping greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. A new instrument, SMAP (Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion), would channel about EUR 15bn between 2028 and 2040 into clean fuels and propulsion.

From 2031 the EU ETS would extend to general cargo and offshore vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnes, partly aligning with the UK ETS. The definition of offshore ship would move to an activity-based test, potentially capturing more vessels serving offshore wind farms. The separate ETS, MRV and FuelEU Maritime reporting systems would be merged into one compliance framework.

The package still needs agreement from the Council and Parliament, with political agreement targeted for Q1 2027 and implementation by 2029, and must be coordinated with the IMO Net Zero Framework.

We cannot do what we do without your support. Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website. More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland. In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP. items.title: Suez return could flip container shipping from shortage to surplus
items.original_title: Suez return could flip container shipping from shortage to surplus
items.summary:
Congestion currently absorbs about 1.7 million TEU of deep-sea container capacity, roughly 5% of the global fleet against a pre-pandemic 2.2%. Schedule reliability fell to 56.4% in July 2026, the year's low, with ships on average 6.06 days late.

As Asia–Europe services move back from the Cape of Good Hope to Suez, that tied-up capacity will be released; one service expects westbound transit to shorten by seven days and eastbound by 14. Around 1.5 million TEU is scheduled during China's Golden Week, 27% more than a year earlier, and Drewry expects 58 blank sailings out of 712 departures.

Rates are starting to soften: Drewry's World Container Index slipped 1% to USD 4,468 per 40-foot box, with a 14 million TEU newbuilding pipeline still to be delivered.

Ultramax and Supramax markets were subdued by Asian holidays, slower North American demand and a lack of Mediterranean cargoes, although period interest continued for five- to 21-month terms.
